stimulus.body: A handover allergy warning is the same size as body text. increasing the warning text above body size gives it prominence, while same or smaller sizes fail to signal importance. A marginal reminder adds: make the warning larger than body. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: A student recalls “Correct type size for a handover warning / Make the warning larger than body. / Type size hierarchy” before answering. Which choice should they make?

options.text: Keep the same size and add colour only
Match the warning to footnote size
Shrink the warning to save space
Increase the warning text above body size

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: increasing the warning text above body size gives it prominence, while same or smaller sizes fail to signal importance. On that basis "Increase the warning text above body size" is the supported choice. Option A ("Keep the same size and add colour only") fails because it relies on colour alone; Option B ("Match the warning to footnote size") fails because it hides the warning; Option C ("Shrink the warning to save space") fails because it reduces emphasis.
questions.hint: Make the warning larger than body.

questions.stem: This task depends on “Simplify a cluttered handover grid / Merge and remove redundant columns. / Grid and reading path”. Which option best satisfies it?

options.text: Add more columns to separate fields
Shrink all text to fit more columns
Merge related columns and remove redundant ones
Rotate the page to landscape

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: merging related columns and removing redundancies simplifies the grid without shrinking text or adding columns. On that basis "Merge related columns and remove redundant ones" is the supported choice. Option A ("Add more columns to separate fields") fails because it increases clutter; Option B ("Shrink all text to fit more columns") fails because it harms readability; Option D ("Rotate the page to landscape") fails because it avoids the real problem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose evidence loss from tight spacing

stimulus.body: A handover prints vitals with no space between lines, and a low oxygen value was missed. tight line spacing merges vitals into a dense block, making individual values like low oxygen easy to skip. A marginal reminder adds: add line spacing for scanability. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “Diagnose evidence loss from tight spacing / Add line spacing for scanability. / Whitespace and evidence” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

options.text: The font was too decorative
The value was printed in colour
Lines were too tightly spaced to scan
The nurse read too fast
options.misconception: selects "The nurse read too fast" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: tight line spacing merges vitals into a dense block, making individual values like low oxygen easy to skip. On that basis "Lines were too tightly spaced to scan" is the supported choice. Option A ("The font was too decorative") fails because it blames style not spacing; Option B ("The value was printed in colour") fails because it introduces irrelevant cause; Option D ("The nurse read too fast") fails because it selects "The nurse read too fast" where whitespace and evidence requires a different condition.

questions.stem: Set against “Evaluate right-alignment of labels / Labels scan better left-aligned. / Alignment and hierarchy”, which choice is actually backed by the text?

options.text: It matches numeric columns
It saves space on the left side
options.misconception: is a minor benefit not a reason

options.text: It creates a ragged left edge that is hard to scan
It centres the page visually

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: right-aligning long labels creates a ragged left edge that disrupts scanning, while numbers benefit from right alignment. On that basis "It creates a ragged left edge that is hard to scan" is the supported choice. Option A ("It matches numeric columns") fails because it confuses labels with numbers; Option B ("It saves space on the left side") fails because it is a minor benefit not a reason; Option D ("It centres the page visually") fails because it misidentifies the effect.
